paragraphs: Those men boarded their ship and set out over the sea. Meanwhile the son of Atreus told the people to purify themselves, and they did so, throwing their filth into the sea. On the sea-shore they made great sacrifices of bulls and goats without blemish, and the smoke of the offering, with its savory smell, curled up toward heaven.

So they busied themselves all through the host. But Agamemnon had not forgotten the threat he had made against Achilles. He called his trusty messengers and squires, Talthybius and Eurybates. “Go to the tent of Achilles, son of Peleus,” he said. “Take Briseis by the hand and bring her here. If he will not give her up, I will come with others and take her myself—and that will press him harder.”

He gave them further strict orders and sent them off. They went sorrowfully along the seaside until they reached the tents and ships of the Myrmidons. There they found Achilles sitting beside his tent and his ships, and he was displeased to see them. They stood before him in fear and reverence and did not say a word. But he knew them and said, “Welcome, heralds, messengers of gods and men. Come closer. My quarrel is not with you but with Agamemnon, who has sent you for the girl Briseis. Patroclus, bring her out and hand her over to them. But let these two be my witnesses before the blessed gods, before mortal men, and before the fierceness of Agamemnon’s anger: if there is ever again a need for me to save the people from ruin, they will seek me and they will not find me. Agamemnon is mad with rage. He does not know how to look both before and after, so that the Achaeans might fight safely by their ships.”

Patroclus did what his dear comrade had told him. He brought Briseis out of the tent and gave her to the heralds, who took her with them to the ships of the Achaeans—and the woman did not want to go. Then Achilles went off alone to the shore of the hoary sea. He wept and looked out over the boundless waste of waters. Raising his hands, he prayed to his immortal mother. “Mother,” he cried, “you bore me to live only a short season. Surely Zeus, who thunders from Olympus, could have made that short life glorious. He has not. Agamemnon, son of Atreus, has dishonored me and taken my prize from me by force.”

He wept aloud as he spoke, and his mother heard him where she sat in the depths of the sea beside her father, the old man. At once she rose out of the waves like a gray mist. She sat down in front of him as he stood weeping, stroked him with her hand, and said, “My son, why are you weeping? What grieves you? Do not hide it from me. Tell me, so that we can know it together.”

Achilles sighed deeply and said, “You know it already. Why should I tell you what you know well? We went to Thebe, the strong city of Eetion, sacked it, and brought the spoil back here. The sons of the Achaeans divided it fairly among themselves, and they chose lovely Chryseis as the prize for Agamemnon. Then Chryses, priest of Apollo, came to the ships of the Achaeans to free his daughter. He brought a great ransom, and in his hand he carried the scepter of Apollo, wreathed with a suppliant’s wreath. He begged the Achaeans, and most of all the two sons of Atreus, who were their chiefs.

“All the rest of the Achaeans, with one voice, wanted to respect the priest and accept the ransom he offered. Agamemnon did not. He spoke fiercely to Chryses and sent him roughly away. So the priest went back in anger, and Apollo, who loved him dearly, heard his prayer. The god sent a deadly dart against the Argives, and the people died in heaps, one on top of another, for the arrows flew everywhere through the wide host of the Achaeans. At last a seer, with full knowledge, explained the oracles of Apollo to us. I was the first to say that we should appease the god. Then the son of Atreus rose in anger and made a threat, and he has since carried it out. The Achaeans are now taking the girl by ship to Chryse and sending sacrificial gifts to the god. But the heralds have only just taken from my tent the daughter of Briseus, whom the Achaeans had awarded to me.

“So help your brave son, if you are able. Go to Olympus, and if you have ever done Zeus a service in word or deed, ask for his help. Often in my father’s house I have heard you boast that you alone of the immortals saved the son of Cronus from ruin, when the others—Hera, Poseidon, and Pallas Athena—would have put him in bonds. It was you, goddess, who freed him, by calling to Olympus the hundred-handed monster whom the gods call Briareus but men call Aegaeon, for he is stronger even than his father. When he took his seat in all his glory beside the son of Cronus, the other gods were afraid and did not bind Zeus. Go to him now, remind him of all this, clasp his knees, and ask him to help the Trojans. Let the Achaeans be hemmed in at the sterns of their ships and die on the sea-shore, so that they may have whatever joy they can get from their king, and so that Agamemnon may regret his blindness in insulting the foremost of the Achaeans.”

Thetis wept and answered, “My son, how unhappy I am that I ever bore you or nursed you. If only you had lived out your span at your ships free from all sorrow, for it is all too short. Alas, that you should be short of life and long of sorrow beyond your peers. It was a cruel hour in which I bore you. Nevertheless I will go to the snowy heights of Olympus and tell this tale to Zeus, if he will hear our prayer. Meanwhile stay where you are with your ships, nurse your anger against the Achaeans, and keep out of the fighting. Zeus went yesterday to Oceanus, to a feast among the Ethiopians, and the other gods went with him. He will return to Olympus in twelve days. Then I will go to his house with its floor of bronze and beg him, and I do not doubt that I can persuade him.”

With that she left him, still furious over the loss of the girl who had been taken from him. Meanwhile Odysseus reached Chryse with the sacrificial animals. When they were inside the harbor, they furled the sails and laid them in the ship’s hold. They slackened the forestays, lowered the mast into its place, and rowed the ship to the spot where they wanted her to lie. There they threw out the mooring-stones and made the hawsers fast. Then they climbed out onto the sea-shore and unloaded the offering for Apollo. Chryseis also left the ship, and Odysseus led her to the altar to put her in her father’s hands. “Chryses,” he said, “King Agamemnon has sent me to bring your child back to you, and to offer sacrifice to Apollo on behalf of the Danaans. We want to win over the god, who has now brought sorrow on the Argives.”

With these words he gave the girl to her father, who received her gladly. They set the holy offering in order around the altar of the god. They washed their hands and took up the barley-meal to sprinkle over the victims, while Chryses lifted up his hands and prayed aloud for them. “Hear me,” he cried, “god of the silver bow, who protect Chryse and holy Cilla and rule Tenedos with your might. You heard me before when I prayed, and you pressed hard on the Achaeans. Hear me again now, and keep this terrible plague away from the Danaans.”

So he prayed, and Apollo heard his prayer. When they had finished praying and sprinkling the barley-meal, they pulled back the heads of the victims, killed them, and flayed them. They cut out the thigh-bones and wrapped them in two layers of fat, with pieces of raw meat on top. Chryses laid these on the wood fire and poured wine over them, while the young men stood near him with five-pronged spits in their hands. When the thigh-bones were burned and they had tasted the inner meats, they cut up the rest small, put the pieces on the spits, and roasted them until done, then drew them off. When the work was finished and the feast was ready, they ate, and every man had his full share, so that all were satisfied. After they had had enough to eat and drink, pages filled the mixing-bowl with wine and water and handed it around, after giving every man his drink-offering.

All day long the young men worshipped the god with song, hymning him and singing the joyful paean, and the god took pleasure in their voices. When the sun went down and darkness came, they lay down to sleep by the stern cables of the ship. When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, they set sail again for the host of the Achaeans. Apollo sent them a fair wind, so they raised their mast and hoisted their white sails. The wind filled the sail, and the ship flew through the deep blue water, with the foam hissing against her bows as she sped on. When they reached the wide-stretching host of the Achaeans, they drew the vessel up onto the sands, high and dry, and set her strong props beneath her. Then they went off to their own tents and ships.
But Achilles stayed at his ships and nursed his anger. He did not go to the honorable assembly, and he did not go out to fight. He gnawed at his own heart, pining for battle and the war cry.

After twelve days the immortal gods came back to Olympus in a body, with Zeus leading the way. Thetis had not forgotten the task her son had given her. She rose from under the sea and went up through great heaven in the early morning to Olympus. There she found the mighty son of Cronus sitting all alone on its topmost ridges. She sat down in front of him, seized his knees with her left hand, and with her right caught him under the chin. Then she begged him, saying:—

“Father Zeus, if I ever did you a service in word or deed among the immortals, hear my prayer and honor my son, whose life is to be cut short so early. King Agamemnon has dishonored him by taking his prize and keeping her. Honor him yourself, then, Olympian lord of counsel, and give victory to the Trojans until the Achaeans give my son his due and load him with riches to make up for it.”

Zeus sat silent for a while and said nothing, but Thetis kept her firm hold of his knees and begged him a second time. “Nod your head,” she said, “and promise me for certain, or else refuse me—you have nothing to fear—so that I may learn how much you scorn me.”

Zeus was deeply troubled at this and answered, “It will bring me trouble if you set me quarreling with Hera, for she will provoke me with her taunting speeches. Even now she is always railing at me in front of the other gods and accusing me of helping the Trojans. Go back now, before she finds out. I will think the matter over and bring it about as you wish. Look, I nod my head so that you may believe me. This is the most solemn promise I can give to any god. When I have nodded my head, I never take back my word, or deceive, or fail to do what I have said.”
As he spoke, the son of Cronus bowed his dark brows. The ambrosial locks swayed on his immortal head, and vast Olympus shook.

Having made their plans, the two parted—Zeus to his house, while the goddess left the splendor of Olympus and plunged into the depths of the sea. The gods rose from their seats at the coming of their father. Not one of them dared to stay sitting, but all stood up as he came among them. So he took his seat there. But Hera saw him and knew that he and the old merman’s daughter, silver-footed Thetis, had been hatching mischief, and she began at once to scold him. “Trickster,” she cried, “which of the gods have you been taking into your counsels now? You are always settling matters in secret behind my back. If you can help it, you have never yet told me a word of your intentions.”

“Hera,” replied the father of gods and men, “do not expect to hear every one of my plans. You are my wife, yet you would struggle to understand them. Whenever it is right for you to know, you will hear it before any other god or man. But if I choose to keep something to myself, you are not to pry or ask me questions.”

“Dread son of Cronus,” answered Hera, “what are you saying? I? Pry and ask questions? Never. I let you have your own way in everything. Still, I strongly suspect that the old merman’s daughter Thetis has talked you over, for she was with you this very morning, holding your knees. I believe you have promised her that you will give glory to Achilles and kill many people at the ships of the Achaeans.”

“Wife,” said Zeus, “I can do nothing without your suspecting me and finding it out. You will gain nothing by it. I will only dislike you the more, and it will go harder with you. Granted that it is as you say, I mean to have it so. Sit down and hold your tongue as I order you. If I once begin to lay my hands on you, it will do you no good, though all heaven were on your side.”

Hera was frightened at this, so she curbed her stubborn will and sat down in silence. But the heavenly beings were uneasy throughout the house of Zeus, until the cunning workman Hephaestus began trying to calm his mother Hera. “It will be intolerable,” he said, “if you two fall to wrangling and set heaven in an uproar over a pack of mortals. If such ill counsels are going to win out, we shall have no pleasure at our banquet. So let me advise my mother—and she must know herself that it will be better—to make friends with my dear father Zeus, so that he does not scold her again and disturb our feast. If the Olympian Thunderer wants to hurl us all from our seats, he can, for he is by far the strongest. So give him fair words, and he will soon be in a good humor with us.”

As he spoke, he took a double cup of nectar and put it in his mother’s hand. “Cheer up, my dear mother,” he said, “and make the best of it. I love you dearly, and I would be very sorry to see you get a thrashing. However grieved I might be, I could not help, for there is no standing against Zeus. Once before, when I was trying to help you, he caught me by the foot and flung me from the heavenly threshold. I fell all day long, from morning until evening. At sunset I landed on the island of Lemnos, and there I lay with very little life left in me, until the Sintians came and tended me.”

This made Hera smile, and smiling, she accepted the cup from her son’s hands. Hephaestus then drew sweet nectar from the mixing-bowl and poured for the other gods, going around from left to right. When the blessed gods saw him bustling through the heavenly mansion, they broke into loud laughter.

So they feasted through the livelong day until the going down of the sun, and every one had his full share, so that all were satisfied. Apollo struck his lyre, and the Muses lifted up their sweet voices, calling and answering one another. When the sun’s glorious light had faded, they went home to bed, each in his own abode, which lame Hephaestus with his consummate skill had fashioned for them. Zeus, the Olympian lord of thunder, went to the bed where he always slept. When he had got into it, he went to sleep, with Hera of the golden throne by his side.
